questions.problem:
Find the value of the constant $b$ that make the function $g(x)$ below continuous at $x=1.$

$$
g(x)=\{\begin{aligned}x-2, & x\le 1 \\ {b}^{2}+2xb, & x>1\end{aligned}
$$
questions.worked_solution:
At $x=1,$ the left-sided limit is

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to {1}^{-}}g(x) & =g(1) \\  & =1-2 \\  & =-1,\end{aligned}
$$

 

and the right-sided limit is

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to {1}^{+}}g(x) & ={lim}_{x\to {1}^{+}}({b}^{2}+2xb) \\  & ={b}^{2}+2(1)b \\  & ={b}^{2}+2b.\end{aligned}
$$

In order for $g(x)$ to be continuous at $x=1,$ we require that

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to {1}^{-}}g(x) & ={lim}_{x\to {1}^{+}}g(x) \\ -1 & ={b}^{2}+2b \\ {b}^{2}+2b+1 & =0 \\ (b+1)^{2} & =0 \\ \sqrt{(b+1)^{2}} & =\sqrt{0} \\ |b+1| & =0 \\ b & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $g(x)$ is continuous at $x=1$ for $b=-1.$

Find the value of the constant $k$ that make the function $f(x)$ below continuous at $x=-1.$

$$
f(x)=\{\begin{aligned}k{x}^{2}+5x-2k, & x\le -1 \\ 4x+3, & x>-1\end{aligned}
$$
questions.worked_solution:
At $x=-1,$ the left-sided limit is

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to {(-1)}^{-}}f(x) & =f(-1) \\  & =k{(-1)}^{2}+5(-1)-2k \\  & =k-5-2k \\  & =-k-5,\end{aligned}
$$

and the right-sided limit is

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to {(-1)}^{+}}f(x) & ={lim}_{x\to {(-1)}^{+}}(4x+3) \\  & =4(-1)+3 \\  & =-4+3 \\  & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

In order for $f(x)$ to be continuous at $x=-1,$ we require that

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to {(-1)}^{-}}f(x) & ={lim}_{x\to {(-1)}^{+}}f(x) \\ -k-5 & =-1 \\ -k & =4 \\ k & =-4.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $f(x)$ is continuous at $x=-1$ for $k=-4.$

questions.problem:
Find the values of the constants $a$ and $b$ that make the function $g(x)$ below continuous at $x=-2$ and $x=0.$

$$
g(x)=\{\begin{aligned}-x, & x\le -2 \\ a{x}^{2}+b, & -2<x<0 \\ 6, & x\ge 0\end{aligned}
$$
questions.worked_solution:
At $x=-2,$ the left-sided limit is

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (-2)^{-}}g(x) & =g(-2) \\  & =-(-2) \\  & =2,\end{aligned}
$$

and the right-sided limit is

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (-2)^{+}}g(x) & ={lim}_{x\to (-2)^{+}}(a{x}^{2}+b) \\  & =a(-2)^{2}+b \\  & =4a+b.\end{aligned}
$$

In order for $g(x)$ to be continuous at $x=-2,$ we require that

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (-2)^{-}}g(x) & ={lim}_{x\to (-2)^{+}}g(x) \\ 2 & =4a+b\end{aligned}
$$

On the other hand, at $x=0,$ the left-sided limit is

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to {0}^{-}}g(x) & ={lim}_{x\to {0}^{-}}(a{x}^{2}+b) \\  & =a(0)^{2}+b \\  & =0+b \\  & =b,\end{aligned}
$$

and the right-sided limit is

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to {0}^{+}}g(x) & =g(0) \\  & =6.\end{aligned}
$$

In order for $g(x)$ to be continuous at $x=0,$ we require that

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to {0}^{-}}g(x) & ={lim}_{x\to {0}^{+}}g(x) \\ b & =6.\end{aligned}
$$

Let's solve the following system of equations

$$
\{\begin{aligned}4a+b=2 \\ b=6.\end{aligned}
$$

We can replace $b$ by $6$ in the first equation. Therefore, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}4a+b & =2 \\ 4a+6 & =2 \\ 4a & =-4 \\ a & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $g(x)$ is continuous at $x=-2$ and $x=0$ for $a=-1$ and $b=6.$

questions.problem:
Find the values of the constants $a$ and $b$ that make the function $f(x)$ below continuous at $x=-1$ and $x=2.$

$$
f(x)=\{\begin{aligned}-5, & x\le -1 \\ 2ax+3b, & -1<x\le 2 \\ 4, & x>2\end{aligned}
$$
questions.worked_solution:
At $x=-1,$ the left-sided limit is

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to {(-1)}^{-}}f(x) & =f(-1) \\  & =-5,\end{aligned}
$$

and the right-sided limit is

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to {(-1)}^{+}}f(x) & ={lim}_{x\to {(-1)}^{+}}(2ax+3b) \\  & =2a(-1)+3b \\  & =-2a+3b.\end{aligned}
$$

In order for $f(x)$ to be continuous at $x=-1,$ we require that

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (-1)^{-}}f(x) & ={lim}_{x\to (-1)^{+}}f(x) \\ -5 & =-2a+3b \\ 2a-3b & =5.\end{aligned}
$$

On the other hand, at $x=2,$ the left-sided limit is

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to {2}^{-}}f(x) & ={lim}_{x\to {2}^{-}}(2ax+3b) \\  & =2a(2)+3b \\  & =4a+3b,\end{aligned}
$$

and the right-sided limit is

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to {2}^{+}}f(x) & ={lim}_{x\to {2}^{+}}4=4.\end{aligned}
$$

In order for $f(x)$ to be continuous at $x=2,$ we require that

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to {2}^{-}}f(x) & ={lim}_{x\to {2}^{+}}f(x) \\ 4a+3b & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

Let's solve the following system of equations

$$
\{\begin{aligned}2a-3b=5 \\ 4a+3b=4.\end{aligned}
$$

Adding both equations we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}6a & =9 \\ a & =\frac{9}{6} \\ a & =\frac{3}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can replace $a$ by $\frac{3}{2}$ into the first equation. Therefore, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}2(\frac{3}{2})-3b & =5 \\ 3-3b & =5 \\ -3b & =2 \\ b & =-\frac{2}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $f(x)$ is continuous at $x=-1$ and $x=2$ for $a=\frac{3}{2}$ and $b=-\frac{2}{3}.$

In order for $g(x)$ to be continuous at $x=2,$ we require that

$$
\begin{aligned}{3}^{4a+1} & =9 \\ {3}^{4a+1} & ={3}^{2} \\ 4a+1 & =2 \\ 4a & =1 \\ a & =\frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, $g(x)$ is continuous at $x=2$ for $a=\frac{1}{4}.$

$$
f(x)=\{\begin{aligned}{log}_{2}⁡(cx-4), & \frac{2}{3}<x\le 1 \\ 2x-1, & x>1\end{aligned}

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to {1}^{+}}f(x) & ={lim}_{x\to {1}^{+}}(2x-1) \\  & =2(1)-1 \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

In order for $f(x)$ to be continuous at $x=1,$ we require that

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to {1}^{-}}f(x) & ={lim}_{x\to {1}^{+}}f(x) \\ {log}_{2}⁡(c-4) & =1 \\ c-4 & ={2}^{1} \\ c & =2+4 \\ c & =6.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

canonical_examples.problem:
Find the value(s) of the constant $a$ that make the function $f(x)$ below continuous at $x=2.$
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14193886/assets/bee9ecfc2bcfaa7741ed1c2aca90b8a077c19715c2a642a9622856f986f434f3.svg)
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
At $x=2,$ the left-sided limit is

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to {2}^{-}}f(x) & ={lim}_{x\to {2}^{-}}(2x+a)^{2} \\  & =(2(2)+a)^{2} \\  & =(4+a)^{2},\end{aligned}
$$

 

and the right-sided limit is

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to {2}^{+}}f(x) & ={lim}_{x\to {2}^{+}}({x}^{2}-3) \\  & =(2)^{2}-3 \\  & =4-3 \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

In order for $f(x)$ to be continuous at $x=2,$ we require that

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to {2}^{-}}f(x) & ={lim}_{x\to {2}^{+}}f(x) \\ (4+a)^{2} & =1 \\ \sqrt{(a+4)^{2}} & =\sqrt{1} \\ |a+4| & =1 \\ a+4 & =\pm 1 \\ a & =-4\pm 1 \\ a & =-5,-3.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $f(x)$ is continuous at $x=2$ for $a=-5$ or $a=-3.$

At $x=4,$ the left-sided limit is

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to {4}^{-}}h(x) & =h(4) \\  & ={4}^{c(4)+1} \\  & ={4}^{4c+1},\end{aligned}

and the right-sided limit is

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to {4}^{+}}h(x) & ={lim}_{x\to {4}^{+}}(4x) \\  & =4(4) \\  & =16.\end{aligned}
$$

In order for $h(x)$ to be continuous at $x=4,$ we require that

$$
\begin{aligned}{4}^{4c+1} & =16 \\ {4}^{4c+1} & ={4}^{2} \\ 4c+1 & =2 \\ 4c & =1 \\ c & =\frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $h(x)$ is continuous at $x=4$ for $c = \dfrac{1}{4}.$

tutorials.problem:
Consider the function $f(x)$ below:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14193886/assets/e46fcaf79d93513c8b946de51ef451ad8a638936681ce3fc70ffdbe8de023078.svg)

The function $f(x)$ seems to have a jump discontinuity at $x=-3.$ However, by selecting a particular value for $k$, we can remove the jump discontinuity and make the function continuous.

We can find this value of $k$ by forcing the left and right-sided limits of the function to be equal at $x=-3\mathbin{:}$

$$
\lim\limits_{x\to (-3)^-} f(x) = \lim\limits_{x\to (-3)^+} f(x)
$$

For the left limit, we have,

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (-3)^{-}}f(x) & ={lim}_{x\to (-3)^{-}}(3{x}^{2}+kx) \\  & =3(-3)^{2}+k(-3) \\  & =27-3k,\end{aligned}
$$

and for the right limit, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (-3)^{+}}f(x) & ={lim}_{x\to (-3)^{+}}{x}^{3} \\  & =(-3)^{3} \\  & =-27.\end{aligned}
$$

Setting the left and right limits as equal, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}27-3k & =-27 \\ 3k & =54 \\ k & =18.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, to make $f(x)$ continuous at $x=-3,$ we need to choose $k=18.$
